segments.title: Why a carrier force needs spare hulls
segments.body: Two carriers are the proposed absolute minimum, with three recommended for a dependable rotation and four to keep one ready despite unexpected failures. France already applies similar numbers elsewhere, with three Mistral amphibious ships and four ballistic-missile submarines. Its two Horizon frigates illustrate another shortage: adapted FREMMs can provide air defence, but their general-purpose and anti-submarine design is judged less suitable for demanding air-defence work. A two-carrier plan can promise continuous availability on paper and still leave gaps when complex equipment fails. The experience of Clemenceau and Foch, and of the British Queen Elizabeth and Prince of Wales, supports the argument for spare hulls.

evidence.note: The opening recommends two, three, or four carrier hulls and compares French Mistral, submarine, Horizon, and FREMM numbers and roles.
The availability argument returns to failures that can leave a two-carrier force without a ready ship, using French and British examples.

segments.summary: Charles de Gaulle is judged a sensible French investment whose main strategic weakness is the absence of another carrier to cover maintenance and unexpected failures.

segments.title: Domestic technology still needs enough ships and support crews
segments.body: French procurement can look impressive when judged by its combat equipment, yet heavy lift and logistics receive less attention. Large subsidies support domestic technology and its promotion overseas, but the criticism is that France then buys too few systems. The Royal Fleet Auxiliary offers a related staffing example: support ships exist, while pay judged inadequate for merchant mariners makes them difficult to crew. Procurement quantities and support personnel determine how much of an expensive military capability can actually operate.

evidence.note: The passage contrasts French combat equipment and industrial subsidies with heavy-lift and logistics gaps, then links RFA crewing problems to merchant-mariner pay.

segments.summary: French investment in domestic technology leaves gaps when purchases and logistics fall short, while the British RFA comparison shows how pay can keep existing ships from deploying.

segments.title: A carrier programme spanning 26 years and several strategic eras
segments.body: Some accounts place the first carrier discussions in 1973 or 1974, while about 1975 is used here for the move towards a concrete programme. Laying down in April 1989 and commissioning in May 2001 meant more than twelve years under construction and roughly 26 years from initial planning to service. Governments, defence ministers, admirals, and senior engineers changed during that period, and the Cold War ended around a design conceived for it. Foch and Clemenceau had entered service in the early 1960s, and successor planning was already taking shape within about thirteen years. That orderly planning cycle still depended on sustained funding and continuity through construction.

evidence.note: The transcript traces planning from the mid-1970s to the 2001 commission and emphasizes changing governments, leaders, and post-Cold War conditions.

segments.summary: The long path from mid-1970s planning to a 2001 commission shows how a capital-ship programme can outlive governments, senior personnel, and the strategic world for which it was conceived.

segments.title: Henry VII and the difference between paper wealth and cash
segments.body: Henry VII's rooms of gold illustrate a kind of wealth immediately visible to contemporaries. In the comparison with Louis, wealth on paper can impress historians looking back at a state's institutions. The distinction is between nominal resources and wealth ready to use. Applied to naval planning, an orderly replacement programme still needs money and execution to produce a carrier.

evidence.note: The analogy contrasts Louis as rich on paper with Henry VII's rooms of gold and applies the distinction to modern governments. Louis is not identified more precisely in the passage.

segments.summary: Henry VII's stores of gold illustrate why resources ready to use can matter more to contemporaries than wealth visible in an administrative account.

segments.title: A carrier as an enabler, command ship, and national symbol
segments.body: A carrier is primarily the platform that makes an air group, command function, and wider task group possible rather than a conventional fighting ship by itself. Its military value therefore depends on hangar space, lifts, aircraft, and the systems that let those aircraft operate. The same logic applies if future aircraft are uncrewed: they still need to be designed for carrier launch, recovery, movement, and support. Charles de Gaulle is presented as a full-spectrum carrier even though it is much smaller than its American counterparts. Nuclear propulsion reinforces its capability and France's claim to world-power status, while logistics remain a practical constraint.

evidence.note: The passage explains the carrier as an aviation and command platform, including uncrewed aircraft, before discussing French status and nuclear propulsion.

segments.summary: A carrier's value lies in the aircraft and command functions it enables, which helps explain why France values its nuclear-powered carrier despite its smaller scale than a US supercarrier.

segments.title: How shipyard politics constrained the carrier's design
segments.body: A dispute between the French government and the country's largest shipyard, along with periods of foreign ownership, shaped the decision to build at the second-largest yard. Naval Group could build the carrier, but expanding its yard would have required additional investment that the government declined. The available yard therefore constrained Charles de Gaulle's size. The British comparison includes the Queen Elizabeth class building dock and its seaward entrance, plus retractable masts for passage under the Forth bridges. Spending on the warship design did not ensure that the government would also fund infrastructure to remove these limits.

evidence.note: The construction account connects the smaller-yard choice and refusal to expand it with carrier dimensions, then compares British dock access and retractable masts.

segments.summary: The construction story shows how political choices over shipyard capacity could shape the physical scale of a major warship before technical design work was complete.

segments.title: Funding pauses, renaming, and a delayed carrier programme
segments.body: The carrier began as Richelieu before receiving the name Charles de Gaulle. A naval act committed the state to construction, but successive governments supplied only limited funding. Government suspensions in 1990, 1991, 1993, and 1995 added to any disruption from strikes or other problems. Entry into service slipped five years from the intended 1996 date to 2001, and construction cost roughly three billion euros. The funding history explains how a formally approved programme can remain expensive and slow to deliver.

evidence.note: The passage covers the former name Richelieu, limited funding despite a naval act, four government work suspensions, a roughly three-billion-euro cost, and entry into service in 2001 instead of 1996.

segments.summary: Political approval did not secure steady annual funding: repeated government work suspensions pushed the intended 1996 service date back to 2001.

segments.title: Why technical expertise matters when judging espionage claims
segments.body: A 1993 Guardian story alleged that British engineers visiting the carrier were MI6 operatives seeking information about nuclear shielding. Rolls-Royce's stated consulting role supplies a reason for British reactor specialists to be involved in the French-led programme. The engineering arrangement is described as a primary design team supported by an external team checking its work. A recollection of a separate British naval-architect visit describes how quickly specialists could recognize design choices because they knew what to look for. Ordinary technical consultation and professional observation offer an alternative explanation to the espionage allegation.

evidence.note: Comparison of a 1993 espionage report with Rolls-Royce consulting and the ordinary observational skill of naval architects.

segments.summary: A 1993 Guardian allegation about British spies inspecting the carrier is questioned against the consulting work of reactor engineers and the observational skills of naval architects.

segments.title: Propeller problems and the 2007 refit
segments.body: The faulty propellers left an uncertain paper trail because a fire destroyed the supplier's relevant quality-management records. The account explicitly says the supplier was not believed to have been intentionally at fault. Spare propellers from Clemenceau limited the carrier to roughly 25 knots, a published figure treated cautiously here. A fifteen-month refit beginning in 2007 included refuelling and new propellers for the stated 27-knot design speed, while displacement rose to about 42,500 tons. Further repairs in Toulon in 2009 show that the major refit did not settle every engineering problem.

evidence.note: Faulty propellers, missing quality records after a fire, the absence of a belief in intentional fault, Clemenceau spare propellers, and the 2007-08 refit followed by 2009 repairs.

segments.summary: The carrier's early propulsion problems illustrate how a complex warship can enter service with compromised performance and need a major refit to reach its intended speed.

segments.title: The cost of a one-off domestic carrier and the lost PA2
segments.body: A domestic one-off asks suppliers to produce equipment they may rarely build, sometimes for the first and only time. Facilities and instruction manuals cannot give workers the familiarity that comes from repeating the job. The comparison with restarting capital-ship gun production warns that early batches could fail while operators regain their judgment of the process. French construction in separated batches is offered as one explanation for Charles de Gaulle's difficulties. PA2 was intended as a Queen Elizabeth-derived second French carrier with CATOBAR launch and recovery, potentially preserving experience and adding availability. Its cancellation left France with the single carrier.

evidence.note: The discussion links one-off domestic production and interrupted shipbuilding experience with defects, illustrates lost familiarity through capital-ship gun manufacture, and introduces the cancelled Queen Elizabeth-derived PA2.

segments.summary: The programme shows why rarely built domestic systems are vulnerable to expensive mistakes, and why a second French carrier would have mattered beyond simple numbers.

segments.title: Reactor enrichment and the decision to refuel early
segments.body: The French fuel is described as high-assay low-enriched uranium, with enrichment between 5 and 20 percent. The comparison uses 20 percent or more for the highly enriched uranium associated with British and American reactors. Lower enrichment is linked here with less power from the fuel and more frequent refuelling, although the carrier's two reactors are described as providing ample shaft power. The quoted 20-to-25-year interval is theoretical, and the earlier 2007-08 refuelling is explained as a way to retain reliable core performance.

evidence.note: The fuel discussion gives the 5-to-20-percent and 20-percent-or-more enrichment categories, compares power and refuelling, and qualifies the notional 20-to-25-year interval with the earlier 2007-08 refuelling.

segments.summary: The fuel comparison links lower enrichment with refuelling and power trade-offs, while explaining the 2007-08 refuelling as a choice to protect reliable core performance.

segments.title: Why published warship specifications need caution
segments.body: Charles de Gaulle's published 27-knot speed is questioned as a complete description of its performance. The comparison sets it beside the proposed PA2's 26 knots and the British Queen Elizabeth class figure of more than 25 knots, with a 32-knot test speed also quoted. These comparisons express scepticism and do not establish an alternative maximum for Charles de Gaulle. The stated method is the "Wiki rule": keep discussion to figures already published openly, with Wikipedia used as an unambiguous public reference. This boundary protects professional contacts and avoids disclosing information obtained through privileged access. Public specifications remain the figures used even when their completeness is doubted.

evidence.note: The discussion compares public speed figures, expresses doubt without establishing another maximum, and explains the public-information boundary called the Wiki rule.

segments.summary: Charles de Gaulle's declared speed shows how to use public naval specifications without exposing privileged information or mistaking official figures for a complete performance envelope.

segments.title: Why food still limits a nuclear carrier's endurance
segments.body: The technical discussion shifts from reactor endurance to the ordinary limit imposed by provisions for the crew. Roughly 45 days of food is given as the practical figure, with French bread, cheese, and wine used humorously to make the logistical point. A nuclear-powered ship may avoid frequent propulsion refuelling, but its people still require stores and replenishment. Endurance must be assessed across the whole ship rather than from its power plant alone.

evidence.note: The passage gives about 45 days of provisions as a limit despite nuclear propulsion, with humorous comments about French food and wine.

segments.summary: The carrier's roughly 45 days of provisions show that nuclear propulsion removes a fuel constraint without removing the human and logistical limits on time at sea.

segments.title: Launcher depth and Charles de Gaulle's own air defence
segments.body: The carrier's self-defence fit is linked to concern that enough escorts will not always be available. Sylver launchers come in different lengths, comparable in principle to the length options for the American Mk 41 vertical-launch system. The shorter A43 cells suit short-range missiles, and Charles de Gaulle is described with 32 Aster 15 missiles. Choosing a longer launcher would allow larger missiles as well as shorter ones. The original eight 20 mm cannon were replaced in 2019 by three remotely operated Nexter Narwhal systems, giving the ship its own gun defences alongside the missile battery.

evidence.note: The passage explains escort uncertainty, Sylver A43 length and missile compatibility, 32 Aster 15s, and the replacement of eight 20 mm cannon with three Narwhal systems in 2019. The unclear six-cell-launcher designation at 35:07 is not inferred.

segments.summary: Uncertain escort availability helps explain the carrier's own missile and gun defences, while Sylver launcher length limits the missiles those cells can accept.

segments.title: Rafales, helicopters, and space for troops
segments.body: The typical air group is described as 30 to 40 aircraft, usually including about 30 Rafale M fighters and two E-2 Hawkeyes. Helicopters aboard escorts help the carrier concentrate on air defence and strike work. It still carries helicopters of its own, including NH90 Caïmans for anti-submarine work and Panther and Dauphin types for other roles. Troop capacity is given as up to 900, with 800 acknowledged as an alternative figure. About 500 tons of ammunition and the troop spaces add transport capacity to the carrier's aviation and command functions.

evidence.note: The usual aircraft mix, escort helicopter contribution, NH90 and other helicopters, a disputed 800-to-900 troop capacity, and about 500 tons of ammunition.

segments.summary: A typical air group of 30 to 40 aircraft concentrates on fighters and Hawkeyes while escorts share helicopter duties; additional capacity includes troops and ammunition.

segments.title: Nuclear-carrier prestige versus usable national power
segments.body: The image of Charles de Gaulle beside USS Enterprise is interpreted as a claim to French standing among the powers that operate nuclear CATOBAR carriers. Audiences can associate the French ship with the scale and power of Enterprise even though Charles de Gaulle is smaller. That association can persist even when a conventionally powered carrier is more powerful. France's existing nuclear industry also supplies infrastructure for sustaining the propulsion choice. Prestige still depends on deployment: a single carrier can be unavailable when a government wants to demonstrate its power. The same ship can therefore be an impressive symbol while leaving a gap in usable force.

evidence.note: The Enterprise comparison concerns the image of nuclear CATOBAR power, French nuclear infrastructure, and criticism of a single carrier's availability.

segments.summary: Steaming with USS Enterprise illustrates how Charles de Gaulle projects an image of French rank, while the single ship's uneven availability exposes the gap between symbolic and usable power.

segments.title: Early availability problems and operations off Afghanistan
segments.body: Early availability problems encouraged French criticism of deployable military power and helped sustain the argument for PA2. Charles de Gaulle nevertheless joined Operation Enduring Freedom with HMS Ocean, two American supercarriers, and Dutch and Italian ships. The air group described for these operations included sixteen Super Étendards, two Rafale Ms, one Hawkeye, and helicopters. The Super Étendards concentrated on reconnaissance and bombing against Afghanistan and are credited with roughly 770 sorties. Those operations demonstrate substantial output during deployment, alongside the separate problem of gaps when the carrier was unavailable.

evidence.note: The passage moves from criticism of availability and PA2 to Operation Enduring Freedom, its multinational force, the 16-Super-Etendard air group, and roughly 770 reconnaissance and bombing sorties.

segments.summary: The carrier's early career juxtaposed periods of unavailability with a real contribution to Operation Enduring Freedom, including strike, reconnaissance, and bombing sorties.

segments.title: Early operating experience and covering allied carrier gaps
segments.body: The early-career tally credits Charles de Gaulle with twelve circuits of the world, 900 days at sea, and 19,000 catapult launches before its 2007 refit. Its ability to operate a Hawkeye adds airborne early warning to the contribution it can make to NATO and other allied operations. Even the United States cannot keep enough large assets ready to cover every disruption. A French deployment that meets the required standards can fill a gap in an American schedule. Such practical cover gives France a useful contribution to offer its partners.

evidence.note: The passage gives the pre-refit operating totals and explains how a capable French carrier can cover allied deployment gaps. The separate training discussion begins at 43:11.

segments.summary: The carrier's operating record before its first refit and its airborne early-warning capability help explain why allies could use a French deployment to cover gaps in their own schedules.

segments.title: Why alliances require reciprocal military value
segments.body: Alliances are described as transactional in the neutral sense that both partners must receive useful value from cooperation. If a larger ally only takes from a smaller one, or a smaller ally only consumes the larger power's resources, resentment eventually undermines the relationship. A deployable French carrier gives France a scarce capability it can contribute when American or other allied schedules have gaps. Shared standards matter because they let partners exchange concrete military support, which helps sustain the political relationship.

evidence.note: The transcript argues that alliances need reciprocal value and explains how carrier deployments can contribute useful cover to partners.

segments.summary: Charles de Gaulle's ability to cover allied carrier gaps supports a wider argument that durable alliances depend on reciprocal contributions rather than one-sided obligation.

segments.title: Why France used American carrier-training facilities
segments.body: Operating Charles de Gaulle required different experience from operating Foch and Clemenceau. French air groups therefore spent time training with the Americans during the 2000s to reach the desired operating standards. American facilities offered extensive areas, sensors, and systems for exercising carrier operations and attacks against carriers. A British proposal to create a comparable training area around the Falklands had appeared inexpensive. The objection was the wear and expense that South Atlantic conditions would impose on the ships using it.

evidence.note: French carrier training with the United States, American instrumented facilities, and the rejected British South Atlantic training idea because of ship wear.

segments.summary: American instrumented training areas helped France develop its newer carrier air group, while a British Falklands proposal illustrates how sea conditions can overturn apparent savings.

segments.title: Operation Agapanthus and a multinational French-led task group
segments.body: Charles de Gaulle left Toulon on 30 October 2010 for a four-month deployment, its fifth major overseas deployment. Operation Agapanthus took the group from the Mediterranean through the Red Sea and Indian Ocean to the Persian Gulf. The French force included Forbin and Tourville, the attack submarine Améthyste, and the oiler Meuse. The listed air group comprised twelve Super Étendards, ten Rafales, two E-2Cs, and helicopters. Demonstrating French presence and reach was part of the mission, together with showing partners what France could contribute as an ally.

evidence.note: The passage gives the fifth-deployment departure on 30 October 2010, its four-month duration, route, French escort and air-group composition, and diplomatic purpose.

segments.summary: The fifth major overseas deployment left Toulon in October 2010 with a French carrier group intended to demonstrate reach and useful military capacity to partners.

segments.title: Allied escorts and covering commitments during war
segments.body: Task Force 473's 2010-11 deployment included a British Type 22 frigate and an American Arleigh Burke class destroyer alongside the French force. The arrangement is compared with later British groups built around a national carrier, core escorts, and supply ships. Allied ships can expand that core during a routine deployment. In a war, the carrier's navy may instead bring ships home from other commitments to assemble a larger national force. The Falklands War supplies the analogy: allies can cover those distant commitments even when they do not join the fighting themselves.

evidence.note: The passage describes British and American escorts in the French-led group, compares later British carrier deployments, and explains wartime concentration and allied cover of other commitments using the Falklands analogy.

segments.summary: A multinational carrier group can reinforce a national core in peacetime; in war, allies can also help by covering commitments elsewhere while ships concentrate for the conflict.

segments.title: From Islamic State operations to the Clemenceau missions
segments.body: French carrier activity continued beyond Agapanthus with operations against Islamic State. The 2019 Mission Clemenceau deployment was named for Charles de Gaulle's predecessor. Its programme included support operations and exercises with Singapore's armed forces. One carrier deployment could therefore combine combat contribution, allied training, presence, and the cultivation of Indo-Pacific relationships.

evidence.note: The transcript mentions operations against Islamic State, Mission Clemenceau in 2019, and exercises with Singapore.

segments.summary: Later deployments link combat against Islamic State with the Clemenceau missions and exercises with Singapore, showing how the carrier combines warfighting and diplomacy.

segments.title: The COVID-19 outbreak and the limits of shipboard isolation
segments.body: The 2020 deployment was cut short after about forty crew members showed COVID-19 symptoms, prompting an early return to Toulon, testing, and medical evacuations. A New York Times report of positive tests among around 60 percent of the complement is mentioned, but the discussion questions that total and raises possible false positives and tests counted across a period. The command and medical teams are described as having overestimated their ability to contain the outbreak aboard. Compartments, quarantine areas, and nuclear, biological, and chemical protection systems gave them confidence, yet the disease had reached the crew before those procedures were activated. Continuous use would consume filters and add cost, staffing, and other management demands. Protective systems were therefore normally activated for heightened threats, exercises, or war, leaving a gap when the virus arrived unnoticed. The later Clemenceau 21 and 22 missions are tentatively linked to renewed efforts to demonstrate presence after the outbreak disrupted the earlier operation.

evidence.note: The account covers initial symptoms in about forty crew, early return and evacuation, a disputed report of 60-percent positive tests, and the activation and resource limits of shipboard protective systems. The subsequent Clemenceau 21 and 22 missions are tentatively linked to restoring a visible presence.

segments.summary: The 2020 outbreak aboard Charles de Gaulle shows how even a highly organised warship can struggle with a pathogen introduced before its protective procedures are activated.

segments.title: Using three Rafale squadrons to sustain one carrier
segments.body: Flottilles 11F, 12F, and 17F operate Rafales, while 4F operates the E-2C Hawkeye. A typical deployment takes two Rafale squadrons aboard, about thirty fighters, and leaves the third ashore. That rotation helps sustain the air group despite having only one carrier hull. France also has three Mistral amphibious ships, which usually allow one aviation-capable ship of that type to be available. Their amphibious and helicopter roles provide a different capability from the strike and fixed-wing aviation of Charles de Gaulle.

evidence.note: The passage names the three Rafale squadrons and Hawkeye squadron, explains the two-aboard and one-ashore rotation, and distinguishes the three Mistrals' amphibious capability.

segments.summary: France sustains Charles de Gaulle's typical Rafale air group by rotating two deployed squadrons against a third ashore, an important adaptation to operating only one fleet carrier.

segments.title: How carrier choices separate regional from global power
segments.body: Regional powers are distinguished from states able to project military influence worldwide, with fleet carriers treated as one marker of the latter category. Britain chose larger conventionally powered STOVL carriers that can visit a wider range of ports and support frequent presence missions. France chose a smaller single nuclear CATOBAR carrier optimized for heavier aircraft and the fullest version of conventional carrier aviation. Global-power status can rest on different design compromises involving operating flexibility, cost, aircraft performance, and availability.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes regional and global powers and compares British port-access flexibility with French nuclear CATOBAR capability.

segments.summary: A comparison of French and British carriers explains how different propulsion and aviation choices can support distinct forms of global presence without making one design universally superior.

segments.title: CATOBAR operations, Hawkeye, and US interoperability
segments.body: CATOBAR, STOVL, and STOBAR impose different compromises in payload, airframe strength, and operating flexibility. STOBAR is judged the least attractive combination here because arrested landings require strong aircraft while short takeoffs still restrict their weight. STOVL offers easier vertical or rolling recoveries for the airframe, with limits on aircraft weight and load. CATOBAR permits heavier launches, but the aircraft must withstand arrested landings. The E-2C Hawkeye is judged Charles de Gaulle's greatest air-group advantage, even above the rest of its aircraft. Compatibility with American F/A-18s and C-2 Greyhounds adds practical value in operating with the US Navy.

evidence.note: The comparison sets out STOBAR, STOVL, and CATOBAR weight and recovery trade-offs, the judgment that Hawkeye is the greatest air-group advantage, and US F/A-18 and C-2 interoperability.

segments.summary: Carrier launch and recovery impose different weight and airframe penalties; Charles de Gaulle's ability to operate Hawkeyes is judged a particularly valuable CATOBAR advantage.

segments.title: Carrier availability and the choice of a successor force
segments.body: Maintenance, salt-water exposure, complex interacting systems, and human error can all remove Charles de Gaulle from service when it is wanted. The central criticism concerns the government's decision to buy only one carrier. If a force of three still lacked a ready hull, that would raise a different question about how its programmes were managed. When Charles de Gaulle is available, France can assemble a capable group around it and demonstrate its reach. One counterfactual pairs a Queen Elizabeth-derived conventional carrier with the later nuclear successor to cover each other's absences, while acknowledging that two ships of the same type would probably be more sensible. The open question is whether nuclear propulsion adds enough capability or status to justify its cost against a conventional gas-powered alternative.

evidence.note: The closing assessment distinguishes single-hull procurement from management failures, considers mixed versus matching two-carrier forces, and poses an unanswered nuclear-versus-conventional successor question.

segments.summary: A capable carrier can still leave France without a deployable equivalent, so the successor debate concerns both propulsion and the number of ships funded.

segments.title: PA2 and the cost of converting a carrier to CATOBAR
segments.body: PA2 is revisited as a Queen Elizabeth-derived CATOBAR design associated with electromagnetic launch. The counterfactual is that French progress on that design could have made British conversion decisions easier because the engineering would already have been worked through. France withdrew early, and subsequent changes to the British ships proceeded without retaining and funding that option. Conversion then required substantial internal rearrangement at high cost. Electromagnetic catapults are described as easier to power from gas-turbine systems than steam catapults, which need a steam supply. A suggested return to hydraulic catapults is mentioned with doubt about whether it could perform adequately.

evidence.note: The bonus discussion explains the PA2 counterfactual, British conversion cost after design changes, electromagnetic versus steam launch, and the doubtful hydraulic alternative.

segments.summary: The cancelled PA2 concept explains why abandoning a shared CATOBAR design made later British conversion proposals costly, despite the relative convenience of electromagnetic catapults.

segments.title: PA-NG's larger flight deck and disputed speed claim
segments.body: Growth in aviation requirements since the Cold War helps explain the larger successor design. The proposed PA-NG is described at 75,000 tons, roughly three-quarters of the displacement of a US supercarrier. Its 310-metre length is compared with about 280 metres for PA2 and the Queen Elizabeth class. The additional thirty metres offers more flight-deck and hangar space, while the illustrated design uses a small single island towards the rear. Two large nuclear reactors are planned, yet the stated speed remains 27 knots. That figure is met with scepticism while allowing that it could be accurate; no alternative speed is established.

evidence.note: The spoken comparison gives the proposed displacement and lengths, extra deck and hangar space, rear island, twin reactors, and a doubtful but unanswered reaction to the stated 27 knots.
The opening links growth in aviation requirements since the Cold War with the larger size sought for a successor carrier.

segments.summary: The successor proposal shown in the 2024 discussion grows to 75,000 tons and 310 metres, with extra deck and hangar space and a declared speed that remains an open question.
